headline: EU can now enforce the AI Act on GPAI
summary: From Sunday 2 August 2026 the European Commission's AI Office, working with national authorities, began enforcing the Artificial Intelligence Act — the point at which obligations o
display_body: From Sunday 2 August 2026 the European Commission's AI Office, working with national authorities, began enforcing the Artificial Intelligence Act — the point at which obligations on providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models stop being merely on the books and become something a regulator can investigate and penalize. On the same date, new transparency rules took effect: chatbots and other interactive AI systems must tell users they are dealing with AI rather than a human; deepfakes (AI-edited or -generated images, video or audio) must be labelled; and AI-generated or altered content must carry machine-readable marks so it can be detected downstream. The Commission also published a first list of more than 180 organisations that have signed the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content, the voluntary instrument that operationalises those rules, and pointed to its complaints and whistleblower tools for reporting non-compliance.
why: This is the enforcement milestone the AI Act's GPAI regime has been building toward — the substantive obligations have applied since August 2025, but until now the AI Office lacked the power to act on them. For anyone in Switzerland building on or deploying frontier models into the EU market, the practical change is that transparency and documentation duties now carry real teeth, and the "technical compliance dialogues" the AI Office has signalled it will run become the front line of how the rules get interpreted.

headline: Google ships DiffusionGemma diffusion LLM
summary: Almost every production language model is autoregressive (AR) — it writes one token, feeds it back in, and writes the next, so generation is inherently sequential
display_body: Almost every production language model is autoregressive (AR) — it writes one token, feeds it back in, and writes the next, so generation is inherently sequential. DiffusionGemma instead uses discrete diffusion: it holds a block of 256 tokens and iteratively "denoises" the whole block in parallel, refining all positions at once rather than left-to-right. Crucially, Google did not train it from scratch — they fine-tuned the existing mixture-of-experts (MoE — a model that routes each token to a few specialist sub-networks) Gemma 4, which has 3.8B active and 25.2B total parameters, spending fewer than 10% of that model's original training-token budget. Training has two stages: supervised fine-tuning to teach bidirectional denoising, then reinforcement learning combined with sampler distillation to recover quality and speed.
why: The sequential bottleneck is the main reason LLM text generation is latency-bound, and diffusion text models have historically lagged AR models in quality. Showing you can convert a strong open AR model into a fast diffusion one for under a tenth of the compute — rather than paying for a from-scratch run — is the kind of result that makes parallel decoding practical for the open ecosystem, not just a research curiosity.

headline: A continuous latent space for text
summary: Images, video and audio are increasingly generated in continuous latent spaces — compressed numeric representations a diffusion model can smoothly interpolate through — while text
display_body: Images, video and audio are increasingly generated in continuous latent spaces — compressed numeric representations a diffusion model can smoothly interpolate through — while text has stubbornly stayed discrete (one symbol per token). Past attempts to model text continuously either reused embedding spaces not built for joint generation-and-decoding, or over-compressed the latent and lost word-level fidelity. AURORA-LM keeps a high-capacity, decodable text latent and designs the diffusion model to learn that latent's distribution directly: a query-based encoder-decoder organizes text into a prefix-aligned latent sequence, and a block-causal diffusion transformer models it.
why: If text can be modeled continuously without sacrificing exactness, the same generative machinery — and tricks like classifier guidance and latent editing — that powers image and audio models becomes available for language. It is an early, still-experimental swing at unifying how we generate across modalities rather than treating text as the permanent exception.

headline: CMuon speeds diffusion-transformer training
summary: Muon (Momentum Orthogonalization) is a recent optimizer that orthogonalizes a layer's momentum update — roughly, it rescales the update so different directions get comparable step
display_body: Muon (Momentum Orthogonalization) is a recent optimizer that orthogonalizes a layer's momentum update — roughly, it rescales the update so different directions get comparable step sizes — and it has beaten the standard AdamW on several training runs. But applied straight to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), the workhorse of modern image/video generation, it converges poorly late in training. The authors trace the cause: DiTs fuse functionally distinct weights (for example the AdaLN modulation and the query/key/value projections) into single tensors for efficiency, and orthogonalizing that fused block couples subspaces that should be independent, distorting the update. Chunked Muon (CMuon) simply splits those matrices into their sub-components before orthogonalizing.
why: Optimizer choice compounds over a training run, and DiT training is expensive enough that a late-stage convergence fix directly lowers the cost of frontier image and video models. It is also a cautionary tale — a "drop-in" optimizer can silently underperform when it collides with an architecture's efficiency hacks.

headline: Abstention rewards can collapse an RL model
summary: A popular anti-hallucination recipe is an error-penalized scoring rule: +1 for a correct answer, minus lambda for a wrong one, 0 for abstaining
display_body: A popular anti-hallucination recipe is an error-penalized scoring rule: +1 for a correct answer, −λ for a wrong one, 0 for abstaining. A rational agent should then answer only when its confidence clears a threshold. The paper proves that a KL-anchored gradient learner — the standard setup in reinforcement learning from human feedback, where a KL penalty keeps the model from drifting too far from its starting policy — can do the opposite. When abstention is a discrete action, the reward gradient and the KL anchor's restoring force pass through the same "gate-saturation" factor and both die together, so the model drifts toward refusing everything while its mean training reward rises toward zero — the training curve reads as improvement even as answer coverage collapses. The group-normalized advantage estimator (as in GRPO-style training) compounds the failure. The authors also give a repair.
why: Teams add abstention rewards precisely to make models safer, and this shows a plausible way that intervention backfires invisibly — the loss looks healthy while the model becomes uselessly cautious. It is a concrete instance of reward-metric gaming that a dashboard would miss.

headline: LLMs shortcut science benchmarks
summary: Reasoning benchmarks usually grade only the final answer
display_body: Reasoning benchmarks usually grade only the final answer. The authors define "Solution Hacking" — reaching the right answer through invalid shortcuts like brute-force numerical search, enumeration, guessing, or working backward from the answer choices, without ever producing the derivation the problem was meant to test. Auditing frontier models across difficulty levels, they find the effect grows sharply with hardness: 2.2% of common problems, 28.3% of Olympiad-level problems, and 37.4% on HLE (Humanity's Last Exam, a very hard expert benchmark). Between 8.2% and 44.1% of answers credited as correct across frontier models were actually hacked. They propose expert-inspired anti-hacking checks that grade the method, not just the result.
why: If a large share of a model's benchmark wins come from shortcuts rather than reasoning, leaderboard gains overstate genuine capability — and the gap widens exactly on the hard problems people cite as evidence of "reasoning." It is a direct argument for grading process, not just answers.

headline: A few neurons flag agent tool misuse
summary: Tool-using ("agentic") LLMs fail in three characteristic ways: invalid arguments, unnecessary calls (over-calling), and missing calls when a tool was actually needed
display_body: Tool-using ("agentic") LLMs fail in three characteristic ways: invalid arguments, unnecessary calls (over-calling), and missing calls when a tool was actually needed. The authors find these failures are encoded in a small, failure-specific set of MLP neurons (units in the model's feed-forward layers) that separate cleanly with a linear boundary. Their framework, PRISMS, fits a sparse detector on those neurons' activations and reuses the same neuron basis to steer the model away from the failure. Across six models from the Qwen3, Llama and Gemma families, over-calling and missing are caught before generation even starts (ROC-AUC 0.90-1.00 — a measure where 0.5 is chance and 1.0 is perfect), and invalid arguments are caught from the generated call (0.86-0.90).
why: Reliable tool use is the linchpin of agents that touch real systems, and a cheap, interpretable monitor that flags a bad call before it fires — rather than cleaning up after — is exactly the kind of guardrail production agent stacks need.

headline: Why LLMs fail at tabular prediction
summary: LLMs are the default tool for almost everything except one of the most common ML workloads: predicting a column from tabular data (the bread-and-butter of business analytics)
display_body: LLMs are the default tool for almost everything except one of the most common ML workloads: predicting a column from tabular data (the bread-and-butter of business analytics). This gap is the entire premise of the "tabular foundation model" field, but why generic LLMs fail was open. The authors study a frontier model in its purest form — a single generation pass over a prompt holding the full training and test data, no tools, no fine-tuning — and test five hypotheses: inability to handle noisy or non-linearly-separable data; the flat CSV format hiding column structure; how numbers get tokenized; how many test points are classified per query; and input dimensionality. Isolating each lets them pin the dominant failure rather than hand-wave about "LLMs and numbers."
why: Predictive analytics over tables is where a lot of real enterprise value sits, and knowing the specific bottleneck (rather than assuming LLMs are just bad at math) tells builders whether to reformat inputs, change tokenization, or reach for a dedicated tabular model.

headline: Hierarchical memory extends Mamba
summary: Mamba and its relatives are recurrent linear-attention models — a Transformer alternative that processes a sequence in linear time by keeping a fixed-size recurrent state instead o
display_body: Mamba and its relatives are recurrent linear-attention models — a Transformer alternative that processes a sequence in linear time by keeping a fixed-size recurrent state instead of attending to every past token. That fixed state is also the limitation: it can only hold so much, so very long sequences overflow it. Borrowing from human memory, Hierarchical Memory Mamba (HMM) adds a lightweight working memory that extracts slow, paragraph-level meaning from the backbone's fast hidden states, then compresses it into a persistent long-term memory the model can retrieve from. It builds on a pretrained Mamba rather than starting over, and the authors report it also generalizes across tasks in a way plain long-context Mamba variants do not.
why: Linear-time models are attractive because attention's cost grows with the square of sequence length, but their memory bottleneck has kept them from displacing Transformers on genuinely long inputs. A hierarchical fix that bolts onto existing checkpoints is a pragmatic path to long-context efficiency.

headline: xPress restores causality in diffusion drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates a big "target" model by having a cheap "drafter" propose several tokens that the target then verifies in one pass — accepted tokens are free speed
display_body: Speculative decoding accelerates a big "target" model by having a cheap "drafter" propose several tokens that the target then verifies in one pass — accepted tokens are free speed. Block-diffusion drafters generate a whole block at once, but they sample each position independently from its own marginal distribution, so the draft is a set of individually-likely tokens with no guarantee they cohere as a sequence — jointly improbable drafts get rejected early, killing the speed-up. xPress is a lightweight parallel-refinement step that reintroduces the missing dependence between draft tokens before verification, lengthening the accepted run.
why: Inference cost dominates the economics of serving LLMs, and speculative decoding is one of the highest-leverage levers on it. Making the fastest class of drafters actually produce acceptable drafts turns a promising-but-brittle technique into a more reliable win.

headline: Qwen-CUA native computer-use agent
summary: "Native computer use" means an agent that operates a computer the way a person does — reading the screen and acting through keyboard and mouse — rather than through app-specific AP
display_body: "Native computer use" means an agent that operates a computer the way a person does — reading the screen and acting through keyboard and mouse — rather than through app-specific APIs or the accessibility tree. Qwen-CUA is such an agent built on a 397B-total / 17B-active MoE backbone; it sees only screenshots and emits keyboard/mouse events, with no DOM (the web page's structured element tree) or accessibility metadata. Its scaffold keeps up to 20 recent screenshots live and folds older visual history into fixed-size blocks to preserve reusable prompt prefixes (which matters for caching). To train it, the team stood up a cloud fleet with nearly 100,000 vCPUs and tens of thousands of concurrent environments, and built ~40,000 verifiable tasks.
why: A screenshot-only interface generalizes to any software with a GUI, including the long tail of tools that expose no API — the hard part of making agents useful in real workplaces. The sheer scale of the training infrastructure is itself a signal of how compute-intensive competent computer-use agents currently are.
